# 📖 Next Word Predictor — LSTM vs. GRU

A word-level language model trained on classic literature, comparing two recurrent neural network architectures (**LSTM** vs. **GRU**) and two text-generation strategies (**greedy decoding** vs. **temperature sampling**).

Given a seed phrase like `"sherlock holmes was"`, the model predicts what word is most likely to come next — one word at a time — trained entirely on the works of Arthur Conan Doyle.

## 📚 Dataset

The model is trained on the **full text** of three Sherlock Holmes novels — not an excerpt — giving it a richer vocabulary and more varied sentence structure than a single short document would.

| Book | Characters (raw) | Characters (cleaned) |
|---|---:|---:|
| *The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes* | 593,911 | 570,750 |
| *The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes* | 600,658 | 530,848 |
| *The Hound of the Baskervilles* | 381,207 | 329,509 |

**Preprocessing pipeline:**
1. Download raw text directly from Project Gutenberg
2. Strip Gutenberg's license/header/footer boilerplate
3. Lowercase, keep only basic punctuation, collapse whitespace
4. Tokenize into a word-level vocabulary
5. Generate n-gram sequences (every line → multiple training examples of increasing context length)
6. Pad sequences to a fixed length
7. Split into predictors (`X`) and integer labels (`y`), using `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` instead of one-hot encoding — mathematically equivalent, far more memory-efficient at this vocabulary size

| Metric | Value |
|---|---:|
| Total words (corpus) | 260,090 |
| Vocabulary size | 12,085 unique words |
| Training sequences | 237,573 |
| Max sequence length | 19 tokens |

---

## 🏗️ Model Architecture

Two models with an **identical shape** were built — only the recurrent layer type differs — so the comparison isolates architecture as the only variable.

```
Input(shape=(18,))
   ↓
Embedding(vocab_size=12085, output_dim=100)
   ↓
[LSTM or GRU](units=150, return_sequences=True)
   ↓
Dropout(0.3)
   ↓
[LSTM or GRU](units=150)
   ↓
Dropout(0.3)
   ↓
Dense(vocab_size=12085, activation='softmax')
```

### Layer-by-layer parameter comparison

| Layer | Output Shape | LSTM Params | GRU Params |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Embedding | (None, 18, 100) | 1,208,500 | 1,208,500 |
| Recurrent Layer 1 | (None, 18, 150) | 150,600 | 113,400 |
| Dropout | (None, 18, 150) | 0 | 0 |
| Recurrent Layer 2 | (None, 150) | 180,600 | 135,900 |
| Dropout | (None, 150) | 0 | 0 |
| Dense (output) | (None, 12085) | 1,824,835 | 1,824,835 |
| **Total** | | **3,364,535** | **3,282,635** |

LSTM has **~2.5% more parameters** than GRU at the same unit count — an LSTM cell has three gates (input, forget, output) plus a separate cell state, while a GRU cell has only two gates (reset, update) and no separate cell state. Fewer gates means fewer weight matrices, which is why GRU is consistently the lighter architecture, layer for layer.

**Training setup:**
- Loss: `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` · Optimizer: `adam`
- `validation_split=0.1` — 10% of data held out purely to measure generalization
- **Early stopping**: monitors `val_loss`, `patience=6`, restores the best-performing weights automatically — training runs only as long as it's helping
- `ModelCheckpoint` saves the best version of each model as a safety net

---

## 📊 Results

Both models were trained under **identical conditions** (same data, same validation split, same callbacks) so the comparison is fair.

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Training and validation loss/accuracy curves for LSTM vs GRU" width="100%">

| Model | Parameters | Best `val_loss` | Best `val_accuracy` | Stopped at |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **LSTM** | 3,364,535 | 5.5969 | 14.81% | Epoch 11 (best: epoch 5) |
| **GRU** | 3,282,635 | **5.4109** | **15.83%** | Epoch 11 (best: epoch 5) |

**GRU achieved a lower validation loss and higher validation accuracy with fewer parameters** — consistent with GRU's typically faster convergence on small-to-medium datasets. LSTM showed a slightly *smaller* gap between training and validation loss, meaning it overfit marginally less in relative terms, even though its absolute validation numbers were a bit worse.

### Why both curves bend upward after a few epochs

Both models show the classic overfitting signature: validation loss drops for the first several epochs, then starts climbing back up while training loss keeps falling. This means the model is starting to memorize training-specific patterns that don't generalize — which is exactly what `EarlyStopping` and `Dropout(0.3)` in this project are designed to catch and limit, rather than being optional extras.

**Is ~15% validation accuracy good?** For context: this model has to pick the *exact* correct next word out of 12,085 possibilities. Getting the right word roughly 1 in 6-7 tries reflects real, learned local structure (which words tend to follow which) — not a broken model. Coherent long-range sentence generation would require a substantially larger dataset and model.

## ✍️ Text Generation: Greedy vs. Temperature Sampling

Two generation strategies were compared from the same seed text, `"sherlock holmes was"`:

| Strategy | Generated Text |
|---|---|
| **Greedy** (argmax) | *sherlock holmes was a very man and i have been a very man and i have a very* |
| **Temperature 0.5** | *sherlock holmes was his hat and that there was your to bring the very man and i had* |
| **Temperature 1.0** | *sherlock holmes was to order to order that he answered you sir about his fall beside this one* |
| **Temperature 1.3** | *sherlock holmes was wilhelm smiling thirteen it clattered which his overpowering campaign s there and lay and at* |

**Greedy decoding falls into a repetition loop** (*"...a very man and i have been a very man..."*) — always picking the single most likely next word routes the model back into the same statistically safe phrase, with no mechanism to break out once it re-enters a familiar pattern.

**Temperature sampling** treats the model's output as a probability distribution and samples from it instead of always taking the top choice:
- **0.5** stays close to greedy but avoids hard loops
- **1.0** samples directly from the model's own distribution — noticeably more varied, less locally safe
- **1.3** flattens the distribution further, favoring variety over coherence — individual words stay plausible, but sentence-level structure breaks down

Neither strategy is strictly "better" — greedy is deterministic and safe, temperature sampling trades coherence for variety. The right choice depends on the use case.

---

## 🔑 Key Takeaways

- GRU outperformed LSTM on both validation loss and accuracy in this specific comparison — with identical data, dropout, and callbacks, the only variable was architecture.
- Both models overfit without intervention — early stopping and dropout were necessary parts of the pipeline, not optional tuning.
- Word-level next-word prediction over a 12,000+ word vocabulary is a genuinely hard task; validation accuracy in the mid-teens (%) is a realistic, honest result at this scale.
- Greedy decoding and temperature sampling make different trade-offs — comparing them directly makes the trade-off concrete rather than theoretical.

## 🚀 Running This Project

1. Open `Next_Word_Predictor_LSTM_vs_GRU_FINAL.ipynb` in **Google Colab**
2. `Runtime → Change runtime type → GPU`
3. Run all cells top to bottom — the notebook downloads its own dataset, no manual setup required
4. Training takes real time (three full novels, ~237K training sequences) — expect each epoch to take tens of seconds on a Colab GPU, with early stopping typically halting training around epoch 10-11

## 🔮 Future Improvements

- Add more novels (*A Study in Scarlet*, *The Sign of the Four*, etc.) — more data is the most direct lever against the overfitting observed above
- Try a `Bidirectional` wrapper around the recurrent layers
- Track **perplexity** as a more standard language-modeling evaluation metric
- Wrap the trained model in a **Streamlit** or **Gradio** app with a live temperature slider
- Experiment with **top-k** or **nucleus (top-p) sampling** as alternatives to temperature sampling
